We ask the same practical question repeatedly: what additional information changes the prediction? Read a real reconstruction and change one uptake bound. Then add environmental dynamics, culture protocols, protein budgets, chemical potentials, enzyme capacities and selected kinetics. Finally retain internal pools and growing machinery while optimizing their control.

The opening follows the lecturer's April 2022 FBA notebook. Both archived BiGG models are included. Every model loads locally. Small declared models make the later constraints inspectable.

Live route: Sections 1–4 introduce the API and nutrient experiment. Sections 5–14 contain optional FBA extensions and model comparisons. Sections 15–18 connect cart balancing, subsystem regulation and whole-cell growth objectives. Run the setup first. The longer optimization comparisons use saved, verified results and include an explicit recomputation switch. The short allocation experiment really solves an optimization during the notebook run.

The biological coefficients of the small teaching models are illustrative unless a source and equation are stated. Read the assumptions beside each experiment before interpreting a curve.

1. Inspect a reaction, a metabolite, and one stoichiometric coefficient

Conceptual setup: core point 7

2. Inspect the objective and the complete biomass column

Conceptual setup: core point 7

The biomass reaction combines precursor demand with energy and other bookkeeping. Its flux is the specific growth objective. Its coefficients are not mass fractions. In particular, large ATP, ADP, H₂O and H⁺ terms describe energy-associated conversions. Ranking by absolute coefficient answers which entries are numerically largest in this reaction's chosen normalization.

Weight the same biomass entries by molecular weight

Does the molar ranking also identify the largest mass contributions? The biomass recipe makes one gram of new dry biomass. For a coefficient sis_i in mmol per gram newly formed and molecular weight MiM_i in g/mol, the signed mass throughput is

mi=siMi1000g metabolite/gDW newly formed.m_i=\frac{s_iM_i}{1000}\quad\mathrm{g\ metabolite/gDW\ newly\ formed}.

No growth rate enters this calculation. Negative values are consumed and positive values are returned. ATP is converted to ADP and phosphate while material is incorporated into biomass. Compare the complete signed balance before calling a quantity a composition fraction.

The net retained mass is one gram, or 1000 mg, per gram of new dry biomass. This requires all 72 entries. Core Figure 6c shows the leading 28. The gross input and output masses are both much larger than one gram because much of that material returns to metabolism. Their difference gives the net retained mass. Under the consumption-negative convention, the signed sum is approximately −1-1 g/gDW.

Leucine has fewer molecules in this column than glycine but contributes more mass. Lipids and cell-wall compounds also move upward in the ranking. These are gross recipe amounts. Computing protein, RNA or lipid mass fractions requires the corresponding polymerization and byproduct accounting.

Change the growth rate: doubling specific_growth_per_h doubles the leucine demand per hour, while leaving its amount per gram newly formed unchanged. The distinction is between a recipe and how fast the cell runs that recipe.

Change the table view: set exclude_turnover=False below to see how ATP bookkeeping dominates the gross ranking. Excluding those entries improves visibility but does not by itself recover polymer composition.

3. Change one bound, solve, and restore it

Conceptual setup: core point 7

An exchange reaction is negative when uptake is allowed in this model convention. A glucose lower bound of −10 allows uptake up to 10 mmol/(gDW·h). It does not force the cell to use all 10. We will compare oxygen availability while holding the glucose cap fixed. The with model: context restores the original state even if an experiment raises an exception.

The optimizer returns the throughput of the entire biomass recipe. Its special flux vbiov_{\mathrm{bio}} has units of grams of new dry biomass per gram of existing dry biomass per hour. Multiplying each recipe coefficient by this flux gives its contribution to the metabolite balance. With existing biomass BB and no biomass removal or death,

dBdt=vbioB,μ≡1BdBdt=dln⁡Bdt=vbio.\frac{dB}{dt}=v_{\mathrm{bio}}B,\qquad \mu\equiv\frac{1}{B}\frac{dB}{dt}=\frac{d\ln B}{dt}=v_{\mathrm{bio}}.

The objective assigns weight one to the biomass reaction and zero to the other reactions. Maximizing the objective chooses the largest feasible throughput of the whole recipe. The code below retrieves that particular flux, checks it against the objective, and verifies the net leucine supply that it requires.

Convert specific growth to doubling time. If μ\mu stays constant, B(t)=B(0)eμtB(t)=B(0)e^{\mu t}. Thus tdouble=ln⁡(2)/μt_{\mathrm{double}}=\ln(2)/\mu. A rate of about 0.982 h−10.982\,\mathrm{h}^{-1} corresponds to about 42 minutes per doubling. The e-folding time is 1/μ1/\mu, about 61 minutes. Changing nutrient availability changes the predicted rate and its constant-condition doubling time.

Python code · In [11]:
In [11]:
oxygen = model.reactions.get_by_id('EX_o2_e')
biomass_reaction = next(r for r in model.reactions if r.objective_coefficient != 0)
print('Before the experiment:', oxygen.bounds)
with model:
    demo.set_medium(model, glucose=10, oxygen=20)
    aerobic = model.optimize()
    oxygen.lower_bound = 0.0  # one deliberate change: forbid oxygen uptake
    anaerobic = model.optimize()
    growth_rows = []
    leucine = model.metabolites.get_by_id('leu__L_c')
    for label, solution in [('Aerobic', aerobic), ('Anaerobic', anaerobic)]:
        mu = solution.fluxes[biomass_reaction.id]
        assert np.isclose(mu, solution.objective_value)
        leucine_demand = -biomass_reaction.get_coefficient(leucine.id) * mu
        leucine_supply = sum(r.get_coefficient(leucine.id) * solution.fluxes[r.id]
                             for r in leucine.reactions if r.id != biomass_reaction.id)
        assert np.isclose(leucine_supply, leucine_demand)
        growth_rows.append({
            'condition': label,
            'objective value': solution.objective_value,
            'biomass flux = specific growth (1/h)': mu,
            'doubling time (min)': 60*np.log(2)/mu if mu > 0 else np.inf,
            'leucine demand (mmol/gDW/h)': leucine_demand,
            'other reactions, net leucine supply (mmol/gDW/h)': leucine_supply,
        })
    display(pd.DataFrame(growth_rows).set_index('condition').round(4))
    display(pd.DataFrame({'aerobic': aerobic.fluxes, 'anaerobic': anaerobic.fluxes})
            .loc[['EX_glc__D_e','EX_o2_e','EX_ac_e','EX_for_e','EX_etoh_e','ATPM']])
print('After the experiment:', oxygen.bounds)

The optimization predicts a lower growth bound without oxygen and a different exchange pattern. A particular optimal flux vector need not be unique. The growth optimum is the primary comparison here. We can explicitly ask for the range of a flux among equally optimal solutions.

4. Change the carbon source and watch feasibility

Conceptual setup: core point 7

Growth on succinate uses a different set of redox and energy routes. Closing glucose uptake while opening succinate uptake is an interpretable change to the environment. The mandatory ATP-maintenance lower bound remains part of the reconstruction. An infeasible case means these combined requirements cannot all be met.

Python code · In [13]:
In [13]:
conditions = []
for name, glucose_cap, oxygen_cap, succinate_cap in [
    ('Glucose, aerobic', 10, 20, 0),
    ('Glucose, oxygen limited', 10, 5, 0),
    ('Glucose, anaerobic', 10, 0, 0),
    ('Succinate, aerobic', 0, 20, 20),
    ('Succinate, anaerobic', 0, 0, 20),
]:
    row = demo.solve_condition(model, glucose_cap, oxygen_cap, succinate_cap)
    row['condition'] = name
    conditions.append(row)
display(pd.DataFrame(conditions).set_index('condition').round(4))
print('Mandatory ATP-maintenance lower bound:', model.reactions.ATPM.lower_bound)

5. Dynamic FBA: let the culture consume its environment

Conceptual setup: core point 8

In a batch culture, extracellular glucose changes. At every ODE evaluation we solve a new intracellular FBA problem. With biomass concentration XX and external glucose GG,

X˙=μ∗(G)X,G˙=vEX,glucose∗(G)X,\dot X=\mu^*(G)X,\qquad \dot G=v^*_{\rm EX,glucose}(G)X,
−vEX,glucose≤10G0.5+G.-v_{\rm EX,glucose}\leq 10\frac{G}{0.5+G}.

The small archived E. coli core model makes this calculation fast. Here XX is gDW/L, GG is mmol/L and time is hours. Oxygen uptake is capped at 20 mmol/(gDW·h). For this depletion demonstration only, ATP maintenance is set to zero. This isolates resource-limited growth and permits a no-growth endpoint. Keeping mandatory maintenance would require a separate starvation or feasibility rule.

Internal metabolites still satisfy Sv=0Sv=0 at every solve. The new state memory is in the external resource and population. This is the dynamic-FBA idea of Mahadevan, Edwards and Doyle (2002), illustrated with a new numerical setup.

6. Add a community environment

Conceptual setup: core point 9

The supplied ecology module uses the same pattern as batch dFBA: solve per-species metabolic problems, then integrate biomasses and extracellular resources. Its primary mechanism follows the carbon/oxygen interaction in Khazaei et al. (2020). Their experiment used continuous culture. Serial dilution is a separate, explicitly constructed protocol in this teaching package.

Species B degrades polymer and releases simple carbon. Species A consumes simple carbon and oxygen. That oxygen removal helps the anaerobic species B. Each species maximizes its own instantaneous growth subject to its small metabolic LP. Both species and all three external resources are dynamic. The organisms, coefficients and curves here are a new illustrative reduction, not a reproduction of the paper's whole-genome models.

Draw the exchange mechanism before interpreting the trajectories. Polymer breakdown supplies simple carbon. Oxygen consumption changes the environment experienced by the anaerobe. This feedback can support different community states under the same feed.

Read the connectors before the trajectories. Solid paths carry material into or out of the boxed double-chevron conversions. Dashed arrows show enzyme activity, from each organism to the conversion it enables. The organism is not consumed as a reactant. The separate dashed oxygen-inhibition path ends in a bar at the anaerobe. All carbon and oxygen inputs join the same second conversion.

7. Choose the culture protocol before predicting the winner

Conceptual setup: core point 10

A continuous culture maintains inflow and outflow. A serial culture alternates growth with an abrupt transfer. A batch culture has neither replacement during growth nor a repeating long-term environment. The averaging convention must be stated when comparing them.

Take two unit-yield consumers with μi(R)=ViR/(Ki+R)\mu_i(R)=V_iR/(K_i+R). Consumer A has a lower half-saturation constant. Consumer B grows faster at abundant resource. Keep the same feed and match logarithmic cell loss:

D=0.15 h−1,f=0.01,T=−log⁡(f)/D.D=0.15\ {\rm h}^{-1},\qquad f=0.01,\qquad T=-\log(f)/D.

This matches cell dilution over a cycle. It does not match fresh-medium volume per hour. The reduced model solves the uptake-limited single-route LP analytically. Its kinetics and parameters are declared teaching choices.

8. Proteome allocation: why use a lower-yield pathway?

Conceptual setup: core point 11–12

High carbon yield need not mean low protein cost. A simple reduction makes this tradeoff visible. Let uu be substrate processing, rr respiration, ff fermentation and μ\mu growth. Use

u=r+f,μ=0.4r+0.2f,0.12r+0.03f+0.5μ≤0.5.u=r+f,\qquad \mu=0.4r+0.2f,\qquad 0.12r+0.03f+0.5\mu\leq0.5.

Maximize μ\mu subject to the uptake cap and nonnegative fluxes. The last inequality is a protein budget. The flux normalization makes its terms dimensionless protein fractions. The coefficients are illustrative, not an E. coli fit. The mechanism follows allocation models such as Basan et al. (2015) and constrained allocation FBA.

At low uptake, respiration gives more growth from each unit of substrate. Its total protein cost is 0.12+0.5(0.4)=0.320.12+0.5(0.4)=0.32 per unit of respiratory flux. The all-respiration solution reaches the budget at u=0.5/0.32=1.5625u=0.5/0.32=1.5625. Further growth requires the cheaper fermentative route.

The network below is imaginary. More respiratory steps illustrate a possible machinery cost. Step count alone does not determine protein demand. Each catalyst points to its conversion with a dashed arrow. Solid paths carry material.

9. Proteome reserve: an upshift needs an allocation state

Conceptual setup: core point 13

A static protein budget does not determine how fast ribosomes accumulate. Mori et al. (2017), Eqs. (2)–(8), retain ribosomal protein mass MRM_R and total protein mass MM. With ribosome fraction ϕR=MR/M\phi_R=M_R/M and allocation fraction χR\chi_R,

M˙=σϕRM,ϕ˙R=σϕR(χR−ϕR),μ=σϕR.\dot M=\sigma\phi_R M,\qquad \dot\phi_R=\sigma\phi_R(\chi_R-\phi_R),\qquad \mu=\sigma\phi_R.

For an upshift to rich medium, the paper approximates σ\sigma and χR\chi_R as jumping immediately to their final constants. The internal state that relaxes is ϕR\phi_R, not σ\sigma. Set final μf=2.45\mu_f=2.45 h⁻¹ and ϕRf=0.50\phi_R^f=0.50, the paper's reported scales. The three initial fractions below are chosen illustrations. The exact solution is

μ(t)=μf1+(μf/μ0−1)e−μft,M(t)M(0)=1+μ0μf(eμft−1),μ0=ϕRiμfϕRf.\mu(t)=\frac{\mu_f}{1+(\mu_f/\mu_0-1)e^{-\mu_ft}},\qquad \frac{M(t)}{M(0)}=1+\frac{\mu_0}{\mu_f}(e^{\mu_ft}-1),\qquad \mu_0=\phi_R^i\frac{\mu_f}{\phi_R^f}.

The assumption that metabolic precursors become nonlimiting is central. The paper explicitly leaves biosynthetically limited downshifts to incomplete medium outside this simple model. This is a dynamic allocation model related to the same physiology, not a claim that static FBA alone generates the recovery.

Reserve has a cost as well as a benefit. For a new reduction based on the paper's Eqs. (8) and (10), take a near-starved initial ribosome fraction equal to reserve ϕ0\phi_0. Set ϕRmax⁡=0.48\phi_R^{\max}=0.48, νR=6\nu_R=6 h⁻¹ and final growth μf=νR(ϕRmax⁡−ϕ0)\mu_f=\nu_R(\phi_R^{\max}-\phi_0). These values approximate the paper's parameter scales. The resulting curves are a calculation from the equations, not traced experimental curves. More reserve gives a faster start while reducing the eventual growth rate. The preferred reserve depends on the duration of the feast.

A distinct carbon-shift model retains translational activity

Erickson et al. (2017), Eq. (5), supplies the related one-dimensional equation for translational activity σ\sigma. It differs from Mori's rich-medium approximation:

σ˙=σ[μfχ^Cat(σ)−σχ^Rb(σ)],\dot\sigma=\sigma[\mu_f\widehat\chi_{\rm Cat}(\sigma)-\sigma\widehat\chi_{\rm Rb}(\sigma)],
χ^Rb=ϕRb,01−σ/γ,χ^Cat=max⁡(0,1−σχ^RbλC),μf=λf1−λf/λC.\widehat\chi_{\rm Rb}=\frac{\phi_{\rm Rb,0}}{1-\sigma/\gamma},\qquad \widehat\chi_{\rm Cat}=\max\left(0,1-\frac{\sigma\widehat\chi_{\rm Rb}}{\lambda_C}\right),\qquad \mu_f=\frac{\lambda_f}{1-\lambda_f/\lambda_C}.

Here μf\mu_f parameterizes post-shift carbon uptake capacity. It is not the instantaneous growth rate, which is λ=σϕRb\lambda=\sigma\phi_{\rm Rb}. The ribosome fraction obeys ϕ˙Rb=λ(χ^Rb−ϕRb)\dot\phi_{\rm Rb}=\lambda(\widehat\chi_{\rm Rb}-\phi_{\rm Rb}). Use the paper's fitted scales ϕRb,0=0.049\phi_{\rm Rb,0}=0.049, γ=11.02\gamma=11.02 h⁻¹ and λC=1.17\lambda_C=1.17 h⁻¹. The particular growth conditions below are illustrative.

For an upshift without pre-expression of the new uptake system, σ\sigma starts continuously at its old value. For removal of one co-utilized substrate, it initially drops by the ratio μf/μi\mu_f/\mu_i (SI Eqs. S52 and S56). This creates different recovery curves from the same allocation rule. The shaded first ten minutes identify a regime this coarse description does not resolve. The paper also excludes prolonged growth arrest.

Why can a downshift recover faster? The second figure reproduces the matched thought experiment in Erickson et al., Supplementary Note 6.2 and Extended Data Figure 9. The pre-shift rates are 0.30 and 0.95 h⁻¹. Both cells have growth 0.30 h⁻¹ immediately after the change and approach 0.95 h⁻¹. Their inherited ribosome fractions differ. Abundant ribosomes accelerate production of the newly needed catabolic proteins. Both responses reallocate protein. This is not a claim that downshifts universally recover quickly or need no proteome remodeling. The shaded first ten minutes remain outside the slow approximation's intended scope.

10. Test a real coupled reaction with chemical potentials

Conceptual setup: core point 14

ATP coupling can favor a reaction without removing its thermodynamic condition. For hexokinase,

glucose+ATP⇝glucose 6 ⁣− ⁣phosphate+ADP,\mathrm{glucose+ATP}\rightsquigarrow\mathrm{glucose\ 6\!-\!phosphate+ADP},
ΔG=ΔG∘′+RTlog⁡aG6PaADPaglucoseaATP.\Delta G=\Delta G^{\circ\prime}+RT\log \frac{a_{\rm G6P}a_{\rm ADP}}{a_{\rm glucose}a_{\rm ATP}}.

Greinert et al. (2021), Table 1, gives ΔG∘′=−17.8±0.5\Delta G^{\circ\prime}=-17.8\pm0.5 kJ/mol at 298.15 K and pH 7. Activities are dimensionless. We choose aG6P/aglucose=10a_{\rm G6P}/a_{\rm glucose}=10 and compare two declared ATP/ADP activity ratios. These are a subsystem feasibility test, not measured cellular states.

The LP balances glucose, ATP, glucose 6-phosphate and ADP with boundary exchanges. Ordinary FBA allows forward flux up to 10 in both conditions. The thermodynamic condition closes that direction when its reaction free energy is positive.

Predict before running: if ATP/ADP falls while all other activities remain fixed, does forward glucose phosphorylation become more or less favorable? The boundary in the plot is a direction-feasibility switch. It is not a discontinuous kinetic rate law.

Change the chemical state: evaluate thermodynamics.reaction_energy(.01) and then .001. A tenfold ATP/ADP change shifts this reaction energy by about 5.71 kJ/mol.

ATP hydrolysis also obeys ΔG=ΔG∘′+RTlog⁡(aADPaPi/aATP)\Delta G=\Delta G^{\circ\prime}+RT\log(a_{\rm ADP}a_{\rm Pi}/a_{\rm ATP}) under a fixed transformed standard state. Usable free energy is a property of the complete conversion and the chemical state. Breaking a bond by itself costs energy. Product formation and concentrations determine the net result. Favorable free energy permits a direction but does not establish its speed.

11. Thermodynamic constraints: exclude ATP from a closed cycle

Conceptual setup: core point 14

Mass balance alone can permit an energetically impossible circulation. Consider an illustrative network with these composite conversions:

A+ADP⇝B+ATP,B⇝A.A+ADP\rightsquigarrow B+ATP,\qquad B\rightsquigarrow A.

Add an ATP drain, and optionally a legitimate fuel-coupled ATP source capped at 2. The two internal reactions can circulate at flux 10 in ordinary FBA. Their net effect is ADP-to-ATP conversion without consuming a net resource.

Phosphate, water and H⁺ are omitted chemostatted species in these transformed reactions. Their fixed chemical potentials are included in the stated ATP-synthesis free energy. The legitimate source additionally consumes supplied fuel and exports waste.

Let d=μB−μAd=\mu_B-\mu_A be the chemical-potential difference in kJ/mol and let ATP synthesis cost 30 kJ/mol in the selected state. The reaction free energies are ΔG1=d+30\Delta G_1=d+30 and ΔG2=−d\Delta G_2=-d. Both active directions would require ΔG≤−1\Delta G\leq-1. Adding those inequalities demands 30≤−230\leq-2, which is impossible. The legitimate fuel reaction has ΔG=−10\Delta G=-10 and remains allowed.

The helper enumerates all four on/off patterns and solves the chemical-potential and flux feasibility problems. In a large network this direction/flux coupling is usually formulated with integer variables. The example concerns thermodynamic consistency, not simply preferring a smaller flux norm.

This is a separate imaginary network, not the hexokinase reaction. Chemical potential is free energy per mole for one species at its current activity. The reaction quotient combines the activities only after summing the stoichiometric chemical-potential differences. The diagram keeps all four reactions, the ATP synthesis cost, the fuel source and the objective in view.

12. Enzyme constraints and kinetic saturation answer different questions

Conceptual setup: core point 15

Two parallel enzymes convert the same substrate pool to a product that can enter a biomass drain. Stoichiometry alone gives product flux 10, set by uptake. Enzyme amounts add individual capacities:

vi≤kcat,iEi.v_i\leq k_{{\rm cat},i}E_i.

Choose normalized turnover constants [105]\begin{bmatrix}10&5\end{bmatrix} and enzyme amounts [0.60.4]\begin{bmatrix}0.6&0.4\end{bmatrix}. The total maximum falls to 6+2=86+2=8. If the substrate pool is only q=0.1q=0.1, saturation adds another restriction:

vi≤kcat,iEiqKi+q,[K1K2]=[10.05].v_i\leq k_{{\rm cat},i}E_i\frac{q}{K_i+q},\qquad \begin{bmatrix}K_1&K_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0.05\end{bmatrix}.

All values here are illustrative and use consistent normalized units. EiE_i is an enzyme abundance whose normalization matches the flux basis. For flux per gram dry weight, enzyme abundance is also per gram dry weight. It is not automatically a molar concentration. Enzyme-constrained FBA can also include a shared protein budget, so these categories overlap. A saturation inequality specifies an additional kinetic ceiling. It is not the same claim as knowing every realized rate exactly.

Biological use: Sánchez et al. (2017), Molecular Systems Biology 13:935, compared Yeast7 and ecYeast7 across carbon sources. An enzyme budget with pathway-specific turnover costs corrected the excessive predicted growth on sucrose relative to glucose. The source fitted average saturation on glucose and still predicted trehalose poorly. This is a source-reported result, not a reconstruction executed in this small tutorial. It overlaps with proteome allocation when only the pooled enzyme budget is used. Full text.

13. A kinetic hybrid can restore selected internal dynamics

Conceptual setup: core point 16

To predict the transient of the substrate pool, release its steady-balance constraint. Keep the downstream product balanced and choose maximal output at the concentration-dependent capacities. The two one-way pathways have independent bounds and no shared resource cost here. Product maximization therefore saturates both bounds, fixing vi(q)=kcat,iEiq/(Ki+q)v_i(q)=k_{{\rm cat},i}E_iq/(K_i+q). Then

q˙=u−v1(q)−v2(q),B˙=v1(q)+v2(q).\dot q=u-v_1(q)-v_2(q),\qquad \dot B=v_1(q)+v_2(q).

Here BB is cumulative product, not a population growth rate. The input steps from 1 to 5 at time 3. Immediately after the step, the new input exceeds output, so the internal pool accumulates. The increased pool progressively activates the enzymes. Its state and history now matter.

This is an explicitly constructed kinetic/optimization hybrid. It shows why a statement about all FBA-related methods needs care: conventional dFBA retains internal steady balance, but hybrids can release selected internal balances and integrate them.

Biological use: Cotten and Reed (2013) captured the reduced biomass yield of an E. coli Δpgm mutant by adding kinetic flux bounds to central metabolism. Those bounds used measured concentrations for the test condition. Ordinary flux balance analysis predicted the parental yield. Performance worsened for another mutant, ΔgpmA. These are source-reported comparisons. The tutorial below isolates the accumulation mechanism with a smaller network. Full text.

14. Compare descriptions before comparing model size

Conceptual setup: core point 17

A mechanistic model composes named processes and states. A constraint-based model selects behavior with physical restrictions and an objective. A learned cellular model fits a mathematical representation from data. These describe different sources of predictive information.

The categories overlap. Karr et al.'s whole-cell model contains an FBA metabolism module. scGPT learns representations from single-cell data. Its learned function does not by itself impose a chemical mass balance. Hybrid models can combine these approaches. Genome coverage alone does not establish which intracellular transients a model can predict.

15. Separate the glycolysis plant from the cart-balancing controller

Choose the extra information by the question. External nutrient change calls for external dynamics. Overflow calls for machinery costs. Nutrient-shift recovery also needs protein dynamics. An ATP/ADP collapse calls for thermodynamic direction checks. A catalyst intervention calls for enzyme capacity. Occupancy or regulation calls for kinetic information. An internal trajectory needs retained balance equations. See the Part 3 model-choice synthesis for examples and limits.

Conceptual setup: core point 4

The nonlinear Hill law belongs to a controller around a catalytic plant. Linearize the Chandra, Buzi and Doyle (2011) example, with intermediate deviation x1x_1, ATP deviation x2x_2, fixed downstream sensitivity gg, and upstream inhibitory action u=hx2u=h x_2:

x˙=Agx+bgu,Ag=[−κ1+g2κ−1−2g],bg=[−11].\dot x=A_gx+b_gu,\quad A_g=\begin{bmatrix}-\kappa&1+g\\2\kappa&-1-2g\end{bmatrix},\quad b_g=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}.

The correspondence uses [θω]=Tx\begin{bmatrix}\theta\\\omega\end{bmatrix}=Tx with T=[11κ−g]T=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\\kappa&-g\end{bmatrix}. Then

Ac=[01κ−(κ+1+2g)],bc=[0−(κ+g)],yc=κθ−ωκ+g.A_c=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\\kappa&-(\kappa+1+2g)\end{bmatrix},\quad b_c=\begin{bmatrix}0\\-(\kappa+g)\end{bmatrix},\quad y_c=\frac{\kappa\theta-\omega}{\kappa+g}.

This is the angular plant of a damped inverted pendulum with commanded cart acceleration (κ+g)u(\kappa+g)u, in a declared nondimensional clock. The matched controller uses u=hycu=h y_c. ATP corresponds to this angle–velocity combination, not to angle alone. The full force-driven cart with position regulation has four states.

Change the gain: compare no feedback, stable feedback and excessive gain in this particular sensor family. The reading core supplies the moving-cart animation. Here we inspect the matrices and both state trajectories.

Python code · In [36]:
In [36]:
kappa, g = 1.1, .3
Ag = np.array([[-kappa,1+g],[2*kappa,-1-2*g]])
bg = np.array([[-1.],[1.]])
Cg = np.array([[0.,1.]])
T = np.array([[1.,1.],[kappa,-g]])
Ac, bc, Cc = T@Ag@np.linalg.inv(T), T@bg, Cg@np.linalg.inv(T)
display(pd.DataFrame(Ac,index=['angle derivative','angular acceleration'],
                     columns=['angle','angular velocity']))
print('Cart input column:', bc.ravel())
print('Matched cart sensor:', Cc.ravel())
time = np.linspace(0,8,401)
initial_x = np.array([0.,.04])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2,3,figsize=(12,6))
for j,h in enumerate([0.,2.4,3.1]):
    closed = Ag + h*bg@Cg
    states = np.array([expm(closed*t)@initial_x for t in time])
    visible = np.maximum.accumulate(np.max(np.abs(states),axis=1)) <= .25
    states, t = states[visible], time[visible]  # local linear range only
    cart = states@T.T
    for ax,values,labels in [(axes[0,j],states,['Intermediate deviation','ATP deviation']),
                            (axes[1,j],cart,['Angle','Angular velocity'])]:
        for i,color in enumerate(['#168b82','#cc6556']):
            ax.plot(t,values[:,i],color=color,label=labels[i])
        ax.axhline(0,color='gray',linewidth=.5)
        ax.legend(fontsize=8)
        ax.set_xlabel('Nondimensional time')
    axes[0,j].set_title(f'Feedback gain h = {h:g}')
    print('h =',h,'closed-loop eigenvalues:', np.linalg.eigvals(closed))
    assert np.allclose(T@closed@np.linalg.inv(T),Ac+h*bc@Cc)
fig.tight_layout()

16. Flux exponent control: retain the catalytic plant and choose activities

Conceptual setup: core point 18–20

The glycolysis example has two evolving internal pools, intermediate qIq_I and ATP qAq_A:

q˙=Sv+[0−w],S=[1−1−12],v1=2qAu1,v2=2κqIu2,κ=1.1.\dot q=S v+\begin{bmatrix}0\\-w\end{bmatrix},\quad S=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix},\quad v_1=2q_Au_1,\quad v_2=2\kappa q_Iu_2,\quad\kappa=1.1.

The catalytic substrate dependences remain. We optimize multiplicative activities u1,u2u_1,u_2 without specifying the Hill feedback laws. The finite-horizon objective penalizes log-concentration tracking error and changes of log activity. The weights, horizon and targets follow the archived 2023 notebook reproduction. Here the demand step is synchronized to time zero and starts from an exact equilibrium.

Demand rises from 1 to 1.1. The chosen target is [1/κ+0.070.93]T\begin{bmatrix}1/\kappa+0.07&0.93\end{bmatrix}^{T}. That target shift is an explicit task assumption. It is not inferred from stoichiometry. State floors are checked. The fast quadratic solve is used only while they remain inactive. No activity ceiling or explicit binding-order polytope is imposed in this particular reproduction.

The optimized activities are not themselves reaction exponents. Binding structure constrains how activities can depend on concentrations in the full flux exponent control theory. This experiment demonstrates structured dynamic optimization and oscillatory transients, not recovery of a unique molecular mechanism.

Read the experiment: activity is the chosen action. Pool concentration is a state that can change only through the balance equation. This example optimizes ATP regulation. Section 17 instead changes the model and asks for final biomass. Comparing their curves does not isolate an objective change alone.

17. Maximize final biomass while preserving metabolic viability

Conceptual setup: core point 19, 22

Start with N˙=(μ−d)N\dot N=(\mu-d)N. For a fixed positive initial biomass, maximizing N(T)N(T) is equivalent to maximizing ∫0T(μ−d) dt\int_0^T(\mu-d)\,dt. An absolute production flux is μN\mu N, not μ\mu. Discounting the running growth reward changes the task. Multiplying a fixed terminal reward by e−δTe^{-\delta T} does not.

The following new normalized glycolysis model tests growth arrest using a pure terminal-biomass objective:

v1=A−2u1,v2=2I,vg=Aug,μ=0.1vg,v_1=A^{-2}u_1,\quad v_2=2I,\quad v_g=A u_g,\quad\mu=0.1v_g,
I˙=v1−v2−μI,A˙=−v1+2v2−vg−w−μA,N˙=μN.\dot I=v_1-v_2-\mu I,\quad \dot A=-v_1+2v_2-v_g-w-\mu A,\quad\dot N=\mu N.

Demand rises from 0.6 to 1.4. The payoff activity is fixed. Controls have bounds 10−4≤u1≤110^{-4}\leq u_1\leq1 and 0≤ug≤10\leq u_g\leq1. An ATP floor is a viability constraint. There is no ATP-tracking penalty.

These saved multiple-shooting solutions use a four-unit horizon and 0.1-unit control intervals. Independent integration and a halved control interval verify the qualitative arrest. They are candidate numerical optima for a teaching model, not a fitted biological response or proof of a global optimum.

Predict before running: allowing growth to pause enlarges the feasible policy set. Its true optimum therefore cannot be worse than the optimum with a positive growth-activity floor. Read the pause directly from the growth activity and specific growth panels. A nearly flat biomass curve alone can conceal a short pause.

Choose one of the saved comparisons below. These are replays of verified optimization results. Set RECOMPUTE_GROWTH=True to solve both selected conditions again. The same plotting cell then uses the newly computed trajectories.

Why compare objectives? Temporary growth arrest and lag are classical bacterial observations. Monod (1949), pp. 386–391, discussed enzymatic adaptation and diauxie. The present ATP-demand calculation tests a possible allocation reason for a pause, without reconstructing every mechanism of a real lag. Core point 21 uses a combined growth-and-ATP-reserve cost. This experiment instead retains explicit biomass and rewards only its final value.

Terminal biomass is not terminal growth rate. Maximizing N(T)N(T) is equivalent to maximizing N(0)+∫0Tμ(t)N(t) dtN(0)+\int_0^T\mu(t)N(t)\,dt, or ∫0Tμ(t) dt\int_0^T\mu(t)\,dt in logarithmic form. It is different from maximizing only μ(T)\mu(T).

The additional horizon comparison replans every 0.1 normalized time units. The 0.1-unit planner reaches a state at time 0.4 with no continuation that maintains the declared ATP floor. The 2-unit planner preserves viability. The short failure is certified by an analytical upper bound on ATP, not inferred only from an optimizer error. The ATP floor is a model assumption, not a measured death threshold.

18. Let growth manufacture its own machinery

Conceptual setup: core point 23–24

The allocation model contains precursor amount PP, metabolic protein EE and ribosomal protein RR. Set N=E+RN=E+R, q=P/Nq=P/N, and ϕ=R/N\phi=R/N. Metabolic protein imports precursor at vin=αEv_{\rm in}=\alpha E. Ribosomal protein produces new protein at vsyn=β(q)Rv_{\rm syn}=\beta(q)R, with β(q)=3q/(0.1+q)\beta(q)=3q/(0.1+q). The control ρ\rho allocates new protein to ribosomes:

P˙=vin−vsyn,E˙=(1−ρ)vsyn,R˙=ρvsyn.\dot P=v_{\rm in}-v_{\rm syn},\quad \dot E=(1-\rho)v_{\rm syn},\quad\dot R=\rho v_{\rm syn}.
q˙=α(1−ϕ)−μ(1+q),ϕ˙=μ(ρ−ϕ),μ=β(q)ϕ.\dot q=\alpha(1-\phi)-\mu(1+q),\quad \dot\phi=\mu(\rho-\phi),\quad\mu=\beta(q)\phi.

A carbon shift changes α\alpha. It does not instantly change the precursor or protein state. Choose 0≤ρ≤10\leq\rho\leq1 to maximize final biomass, subject to q≥0.02q\geq0.02 and 0.02≤ϕ≤0.980.02\leq\phi\leq0.98. No death, protein degradation or other biomass sectors are modeled.

Solve a short experiment live: change horizon or exchange the before/after uptake capacities. The optimizer runs here, rather than loading this short result from a file.

The allocation ρ\rho is the fraction of new protein sent to ribosomes. The composition ϕ\phi is the fraction of existing protein in ribosomes. Their difference determines the direction of composition change through ϕ˙=μ(ρ−ϕ)\dot\phi=\mu(\rho-\phi). A chosen action can jump. Existing protein cannot be reassigned instantaneously.

Compare horizons and the value assigned to future growth

The longer saved solves compare two- and eight-hour horizons, plus the running reward ∫0Te−δtμ(t) dt\int_0^T e^{-\delta t}\mu(t)\,dt with δ=2 h−1\delta=2\ {\rm h}^{-1}. The same dynamic plant supports different preferred allocations. After a downshift, the eight-hour final-biomass objective initially favors metabolic protein. Strong discounting initially favors ribosomal protein.

End-of-horizon resource spending is part of a finite task. It is not a new steady-growth law. Very late controls under strong discounting are weakly determined. Thiermann et al. (2026) measured different growth and stress responses in E. coli and B. subtilis. Their translation-inhibition experiment does not identify these discount factors and is not a carbon-shift fit.

The dotted two-hour marker in core Figure 20c is the planning endpoint. It does not mark loss of feasibility. The two-hour trajectory was computed only to that endpoint. The ATP viability failure above is a different, repeatedly replanned experiment.

Optional control cost. A penalty γ∑k(ρk−ρk−1)2/Δt\gamma\sum_k(\rho_k-\rho_{k-1})^2/\Delta t makes allocation changes costly. The saved comparison holds the eight-hour plant and conditions fixed and tests γ=0,0.02,0.2\gamma=0,0.02,0.2 h. It makes the action smoother and reduces some overshoot, while sacrificing biomass. It is not an experimental fit, and finite-endpoint incentives remain.

Set RECOMPUTE_SMOOTHING=True below to recompute the eight-hour penalty comparison. Change change_penalty in the earlier live cell for a shorter calculation.

allocation_results = json.loads((HERE / 'data/allocation-results.json').read_text())
# Switch between a horizon comparison and a reward comparison.
allocation_comparison = 'discount'  # alternatively: 'horizon'
shift = 'downshift'                 # alternatively: 'upshift'
RECOMPUTE_ALLOCATION = False
before, after = (.3,1.2) if shift == 'upshift' else (1.2,.3)
settings = [(8.,0.),(8.,2.)] if allocation_comparison == 'discount' else [(2.,0.),(8.,0.)]
selected_allocation = {}
for horizon, discount in settings:
    key = f'{shift}_T{horizon:g}_discount{discount:g}'
    selected_allocation[key] = (allocation_control.optimize(
        before,after,horizon=horizon,discount=discount)
        if RECOMPUTE_ALLOCATION else allocation_results[key])
print('RECOMPUTED optimizations' if RECOMPUTE_ALLOCATION else 'SAVED, verified optimization results')
display(pd.DataFrame([{'case':key, **r['summary']} for key,r in selected_allocation.items()]).round(6))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2,2,figsize=(10,7),layout='constrained')
for color,(key,r) in zip(figures.COLORS,selected_allocation.items()):
    x = np.asarray(r['x'])
    label = f"Horizon {r['horizon']:g} h, discount {r['discount']:g}/h"
    edges = np.linspace(0,r['horizon'],len(r['rho'])+1)
    axes[0,0].stairs(r['rho'],edges,label=label,color=color,baseline=None)
    axes[0,1].plot(r['t'],x[:,1],color=color)
    axes[1,0].plot(r['t'],r['growth'],color=color)
    axes[1,1].plot(r['t'],r['biomass'],color=color)
for ax,label in zip(axes.ravel(),['New-protein allocation to ribosomes','Existing ribosomal protein fraction',
                                'Specific growth (1/h)','Biomass / initial biomass']):
    ax.set(xlabel='Time (h)',ylabel=label)
axes[0,0].set_ylim(-.03,1.03)
fig.legend(*axes[0,0].get_legend_handles_labels(),loc='outside lower center',fontsize=9)
fig.suptitle(shift.capitalize()+': same plant, changed future reward',fontsize=14)
plt.show()
print('Compare final biomass only at matched times. A two-hour task ends at two hours.')


# Compare optional allocation-change costs for the same eight-hour problem.
RECOMPUTE_SMOOTHING = False
smoothing_cases = json.loads((HERE / 'data/allocation-smoothing.json').read_text())
if RECOMPUTE_SMOOTHING:
    for kind, old_alpha, new_alpha in [('upshift',.3,1.2), ('downshift',1.2,.3)]:
        base = allocation_control.optimize(old_alpha,new_alpha,horizon=8.)
        smoothing_cases[f'{kind}_penalty0'] = base
        for penalty in [.02,.2]:
            smoothing_cases[f'{kind}_penalty{penalty:g}'] = allocation_control.optimize(
                old_alpha,new_alpha,horizon=8.,change_penalty=penalty,
                seeds=[np.array(base['rho']),np.full(40,allocation_control.steady(new_alpha)[1])])
print('RECOMPUTED allocation-change costs' if RECOMPUTE_SMOOTHING else 'SAVED, verified allocation-change costs')
figures.allocation_smoothing(smoothing_cases)
plt.show()
display(pd.DataFrame([{'case': key, 'final biomass': r['summary']['final_biomass'],
                       'allocation change cost': r['summary'].get('allocation_change_cost',0.)}
                      for key,r in smoothing_cases.items()]).round(5))

Source and model notes

The detailed equations, parameter status, references and verification are in MODEL-NOTES.md and verification.json. Starting sources include Orth et al. (2011) for iJO1366, Mahadevan et al. (2002) for dynamic FBA, Basan et al. (2015) and Mori et al. (2016) for allocation constraints, Mori et al. (2017) for reserve-dependent rich-medium recovery, Erickson et al. (2017) for carbon-shift kinetics, Henry et al. (2007) for thermodynamic consistency, Sánchez et al. (2017) for enzyme constraints, Covert et al. (2008) for kinetic hybrids, Xiao, Li and Doyle (2023) for flux exponent control, and Khazaei et al. (2020) for community multistability. The offline model JSON files were archived from BiGG on 13 October 2026 and copied unchanged into this package.

COBRApy API documentation: object inspection and bound resets, local JSON loading, and dynamic FBA. These links are optional reading. The notebook itself runs offline after its Python dependencies are installed.

Additional sources: Chandra, Buzi and Doyle (2011) for the glycolytic plant and feedback limitation. Feist and Palsson (2010) for biomass accounting. Greinert et al. (2021), Table 1, for the activity-based hexokinase standard reaction energy. Karr et al. (2012) and Cui et al. (2024) for the model-family comparison. Thiermann et al. (2026) for the distinct bacterial growth and stress architectures.

STAGED-MODEL-NOTES.md records the new model boundaries, result files and checks. The culture-protocol, mass, enzyme-sharing and growth-control calculations are new teaching calculations. The full texts and detailed reading records stay in the course literature archive.
